_about: For English speakers: what replaces the comparisons with Dutch on the website (PLAN 9.10). build_web.py applies it; the content files and PDFs stay as they are. 'boxes': whole boxes by '<content file without .json>#<block number>'. 'texts': [old, new] pieces of text inside a block. 'blocks': whole blocks (tables with a Dutch column).

a1_01_pronunciation_spelling#7.title: Tips for English speakers
bullets: Keep each vowel short and pure. English vowels often glide (say, go, no sound like ay-ee, oh-oo). Spanish e and o never glide: no is one clean sound.
Say every vowel clearly, also when it is unstressed: ca-sa, not ca-suh. English turns weak vowels into a schwa (banana = buh-NAH-nuh); Spanish never does: ba-na-na.

a1_01_pronunciation_spelling#20.title: Free vocabulary: English endings that match Spanish
bullets: English -tion = Spanish -ción: nation / nación, information / información, situation / situación.
English -ty = Spanish -dad or -tad: university / universidad, activity / actividad, liberty / libertad.
English -logy = Spanish -logía: biology / biología, technology / tecnología.

a1_02_regular_present#25.title: Good news for English speakers
a1_02_regular_present#25.text: One Spanish form covers both English presents: hablo means I speak and I am speaking. Spanish also often uses the present for the near future, where English uses the present continuous: Mañana trabajo = I'm working tomorrow.

a1_03_irregular_present#14.title: Saber or conocer? Two kinds of “know”
a1_03_irregular_present#14.text: English has one verb, Spanish has two. saber = to know facts, information and skills (Sé la respuesta. Sé nadar = I know how to swim). conocer = to know people, places and things you are familiar with (Conozco a Marta. Conozco Madrid.). Tip: if you could say “be familiar with”, use conocer.

a1_04_ser_estar_hay_tener#3.title: English has one verb, Spanish has two
a1_04_ser_estar_hay_tener#3.text: English to be becomes ser or estar. Ask yourself: am I saying what it is (identity, characteristic) or where or how it is right now (location, temporary state)? The first is ser, the second estar: Soy alto (I am tall), Estoy cansado (I am tired).

a1_04_ser_estar_hay_tener#20.title: Age: Spanish says “have”, not “be”
a1_04_ser_estar_hay_tener#20.text: English says I am 20. Spanish says Tengo 20 años (literally: I have 20 years). Always include años. Other English “be” phrases also use tener: tengo hambre (I'm hungry), tengo frío (I'm cold), tengo razón (I'm right).

a1_05_nouns_articles_adjectives#6.title: English “the” is el, la, los or las
a1_05_nouns_articles_adjectives#6.text: English has one article for everything; Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine, even things: el sol, la luna, el problema, la mano. Learn each Spanish noun with its article from the start, and the adjective follows it: la casa blanca.

a1_07_reflexives_gustar#13.title: Body parts and clothes: use el, la, los, las
a1_07_reflexives_gustar#13.text: English says I wash my hands. Spanish uses the article, not a possessive: Me lavo las manos, Me pongo el abrigo. The reflexive pronoun already shows whose hands they are; mis manos sounds odd here.

a1_07_reflexives_gustar#19.title: Think “is pleasing to me”
a1_07_reflexives_gustar#19.text: English I like cats becomes Me gustan los gatos: literally “cats are pleasing to me”. The cats are the subject, so the verb is plural: gustan. One thing: Me gusta el café; several things: Me gustan los gatos.

a1_08_sentence_structure#5.title: Word order: close to English, with two differences
bullets: Adjectives usually come after the noun: a red car = un coche rojo.
Questions need no helper verb like do or does: Do you live here? = ¿Vives aquí? Spanish shows the question with intonation and ¿ ? only.

a1_08_sentence_structure#9.title: Double negatives are normal
a1_08_sentence_structure#9.text: English avoids two negatives (I don't see anyone, not I don't see nobody). Spanish requires them when the negative word comes after the verb: No veo a nadie, No tengo nada, No voy nunca.

a1_09_vocabulary_phrases#14.title: Telling the time: no “past” and “to” guessing
a1_09_vocabulary_phrases#14.text: English half past two is las dos y media: Spanish adds the minutes to the hour with y, and takes them away with menos: a quarter to three = las tres menos cuarto. And it is la una (singular) but las dos, las tres.

a2_01_preterite_regular#4.title: One past for finished events
bullets: English I worked (a finished event at a finished time) is the Spanish preterite: Ayer trabajé = I worked yesterday.
English I have worked is not always he trabajado: Spain uses he trabajado for today, this week and this year, even with a time like esta mañana (Chapter 5).

a2_01_preterite_regular#8.title: hace = ago
a2_01_preterite_regular#8.text: hace + time goes in front: hace dos días = two days ago. English puts ago at the end.

a2_02_preterite_irregular#27.title: English uses other verbs for this
a2_02_preterite_irregular#27.text: English needs different verbs where Spanish just changes the tense: Conocí a Lucía = I met Lucía; Supe la verdad = I found out the truth; No pude abrirla = I couldn't (tried and failed) open it.

a2_03_imperfect#4.title: English “I worked” covers both
bullets: English I worked can be a habit (I worked every day) or a single event. Spanish splits them: trabajaba for the habit, trabajé for the single finished event (Chapter 4).
Test: if the English can be used to, would (for a habit) or was ...ing, use the imperfect: I used to work = trabajaba, I was working = trabajaba / estaba trabajando.

a2_04_preterite_vs_imperfect#4.title: English “when” can be either
a2_04_preterite_vs_imperfect#4.text: When I was young describes a state: Cuando era joven. When I arrived is a single event: Cuando llegué. Same English word, different Spanish tense. Ask yourself what the verb after when describes.

a2_05_present_perfect#13.title: haber, and nothing in between
bullets: Like English have, Spanish always uses haber: I have gone = he ido (never soy ido).
English can put words in between: I have already eaten, I haven't eaten. In Spanish he and the participle stay together: ya he comido, no he comido.

a2_05_present_perfect#26.title: Spain uses the perfect for today
a2_05_present_perfect#26.text: English says I ate an hour ago but I have eaten today. Spain follows the time frame, not the moment: anything inside today, this week, this year takes the perfect (Esta mañana he comido fruta = I ate fruit this morning), anything in a finished time takes the preterite (Ayer comí).

a2_06_future_ongoing#6.title: Almost the same as English “going to”
bullets: I'm going to study = voy a estudiar. Do not forget the a.
in two days (from now) = dentro de dos días. en dos días means “within two days, taking two days” and is a different idea.

a2_06_future_ongoing#18.title: English -ing is not always estar + gerund
a2_06_future_ongoing#18.text: I'm cooking (right now) = Estoy cocinando. But for plans English also uses -ing (I'm leaving tomorrow), and Spanish then uses the plain present: Me voy mañana. And after a preposition English -ing is a Spanish infinitive: before leaving = antes de salir.

a2_06_future_ongoing#26.title: English “just” and “again”, plus two more
bullets: again = volver a: I called again = Volví a llamar. I've been studying for two years = Llevo dos años estudiando.
Also: terminar de + infinitive (Terminé de trabajar a las seis) and aprender a + infinitive (Aprendí a nadar de niño).

a2_07_imperative#24.title: Negative commands are different
a2_07_imperative#24.text: English just adds don't: Talk! / Don't talk!. In Spanish a negative tú command cannot use the affirmative form: Habla but No hables (never No habla). The same goes for vosotros: Hablad, but No habléis.

a2_08_object_pronouns#6.title: No “it” as a subject
a2_08_object_pronouns#6.text: English needs it as a subject: It's raining, It's late. Spanish leaves it out: Llueve, Es tarde. As an object, it becomes lo / la, before the verb: I see it = Lo veo.

a2_08_object_pronouns#19.title: Order: before the verb, person first
a2_08_object_pronouns#19.text: English puts the pronouns after the verb: I give it to him. Spanish puts them before the conjugated verb, the person first: Se lo doy (to him / it). Remember: indirect before direct, and le becomes se before lo, la.

a2_09_comparisons_prepositions#10.title: than, as and in
a2_09_comparisons_prepositions#10.text: bigger than = más grande que. as big as = tan grande como. the biggest in Spain = el más grande de España (Spanish says “of”, not “in”).

a2_09_comparisons_prepositions#18.title: English “for”: por or para
a2_09_comparisons_prepositions#18.text: English for becomes para (recipient, purpose, deadline: para ti, para aprender, para el lunes) or por (reason, price, in exchange, duration: gracias por todo, por diez euros). through and because of are also por.

a2_10_vocabulary_phrases#16.title: oreja or oído?
a2_10_vocabulary_phrases#16.text: English ear has two Spanish words: la oreja is the outside of the ear, el oído is the inner ear and the sense of hearing. Me duele el oído (my ear hurts, inside), Tiene las orejas grandes (he has big ears).

b1_01_future_conditional#18.title: will = futuro, would = condicional
b1_01_future_conditional#18.text: English will matches the Spanish future (iré) and would matches the conditional (iría). But English often uses going to or the present continuous for plans, and so does Spanish: Mañana trabajo, Voy a trabajar.

b1_01_future_conditional#30.title: would = conditional, not always
b1_01_future_conditional#30.text: English would is also a habit in the past (we would play outside): that is the Spanish imperfect (jugábamos), not the conditional. For politeness Spanish often uses quisiera or me gustaría (Quisiera un café = I would like a coffee).

b1_02_subjunctive_forms#4.title: English uses an infinitive here
b1_02_subjunctive_forms#4.text: I want you to come uses an infinitive in English. Spanish needs que + a new verb: Quiero que vengas. Whenever English says want / ask / tell someone to do, think que + subjunctive.

b1_03_subjunctive_uses#8.title: English “that” + normal verb = que + subjunctive
b1_03_subjunctive_uses#8.text: I hope (that) you come is Espero que vengas; It's important that you help is Es importante que ayudes. In English the verb after that looks normal; in Spanish it changes after verbs of wishing, hoping, feeling and doubting.

b1_03_subjunctive_uses#26.title: English present for the future
b1_03_subjunctive_uses#26.text: English says When you arrive, call me and When I arrive, I call with the same present tense. Spanish distinguishes: Cuando llegues (it has not happened yet: subjunctive) vs Cuando llego (it happens regularly: indicative).

b1_04_perfect_tenses#5.title: Same logic as English
b1_04_perfect_tenses#5.text: had eaten = había comido, will have eaten = habrá comido, would have eaten = habría comido. Just like English have, Spanish always uses haber, and the participle never changes: ella había comido.

b1_05_relative_clauses#4.title: who, which, that and what
b1_05_relative_clauses#4.text: English chooses between who, which and that, and can leave it out (the book I read). Spanish uses que for all of them and never leaves it out: the book (that) I read = el libro que leí, the man who = el hombre que. For what = “the thing that”: lo que (what you say = lo que dices).

b1_06_passive_se#5.title: is cleaned vs is clean
b1_06_passive_se#5.text: English the house is cleaned (the action) and the house is clean (the result) both use be. Spanish uses ser + participle for the action (es limpiada) and estar + participle for the result (está limpia). In everyday Spanish the action is usually said with se: se limpia la casa.

b1_06_passive_se#21.title: English: “I dropped it”
b1_06_passive_se#21.text: English says I dropped it, I broke my phone, I forgot. Spanish prefers se me cayó (it fell to me), se me rompió el móvil, se me olvidó when it is an accident. Rompí el móvil sounds as if you did it on purpose.

b1_07_if_reported#5.title: Same as English
b1_07_if_reported#5.text: If it rains, I'll stay at home = Si llueve, me quedo / me quedaré en casa. Like English, Spanish never puts the future after si: not si lloverá, just as English doesn't say if it will rain.

b1_08_ser_estar_change#14.title: become, get, turn, go
b1_08_ser_estar_change#14.text: English uses many verbs for change. Spanish chooses by the kind of change: he got angry = se puso furioso (temporary mood); he became a doctor = se hizo médico (effort, choice); he went mad = se volvió loco (sudden, lasting); he became famous = llegó a ser famoso (after a long way).

b2_04_periphrases#11.title: Llevo dos años estudiando
b2_04_periphrases#11.text: English uses the present perfect continuous: I've been studying for two years. Spanish has this specific structure: llevar + time + gerund. Estudio desde hace dos años is also correct (Spanish uses the present here, not the perfect).

c1_01_tense_nuance#9.title: English uses other verbs, Spanish the tense
c1_01_tense_nuance#9.text: English changes the verb; Spanish changes the tense. Lo supe ayer = I found out yesterday. No quise ir = I refused to go (and I did not). No pude ir = I couldn't go (I tried, and I did not).

c1_07_idiomatic_verbs#3.title: se = up, all, the whole
c1_07_idiomatic_verbs#3.text: Spanish often adds se to show involvement or completion: Se leyó el libro (he read the whole book), Me bebí el café (I drank it all up), Se comió la tarta (she ate up the cake). English adds up, all or the whole; Spanish adds a pronoun.

c2_03_syntax#4.title: English learners: the subject can come later
c2_03_syntax#4.text: English keeps subject-verb order almost always (John arrived yesterday). Spanish can put the subject after the verb to present new information: Ayer llegó Juan, Me lo dijo tu hermana. And it never inverts after an adverb the way English does after never or rarely: Nunca lo había visto.

a1_01_pronunciation_spelling#9: harsh h, like the Dutch ch in acht
harsh h, like the ch in Scottish loch
Dutch speakers already have this sound
English has no such sound: say the ch of loch, firmly
like the y in yes (Dutch j); the word
like the y in yes; the word
like the y in yes (Dutch j)
ny, as in canyon (Dutch nj in oranje)
ny, as in canyon or onion
like the ch in church (Dutch tsj)
a1_01_pronunciation_spelling#19: Never double a vowel the way Dutch does: hablar, not hablaar.
Vowels are never doubled to make them long: hablar, not hablaar, and tú, not too.
a2_09_comparisons_prepositions#16: which makes them hard for Dutch speakers (voor)
which makes them hard for English speakers
b1_05_relative_clauses#0: avoid the most common Dutch-influenced mistakes with relative clauses
avoid the most common mistakes English speakers make with relative clauses
b1_07_if_reported#15: Dutch speakers often make this mistake because they think of zou twice (als ik tijd zou hebben, zou ik gaan).
English speakers sometimes make this mistake because they think of would twice (if I would have time, I would go).
